# Is it safe?

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

source("R/book_setup.R")
```

The first thing people say is that it is cute.

Very cute, usually, because it is so different from what anyone expects a car to look like. That was especially true in 2010. Smarts were not common then, and pulling into a gas station meant somebody was going to come over.

*I like your car.* That was almost always the opener. **Seeing TwoRed was an invitation to talk**, and a great many conversations started exactly that way, with a stranger walking across a forecourt to say something friendly about a very small car.

@fig-day-one is TwoRed on the first day we owned it. **That is the car people were crossing forecourts to look at** — small, bright, and not much like anything else in the row.

**It did not last, and the record of that is worth keeping.** By the time we were driving Creamsicle, Smart cars were relatively common and the effect had largely worn off. People no longer crossed a forecourt to look. Creamsicle is cute too — **but by my measure not quite as cute as TwoRed**, and in any case by then it was not a surprise. **The reaction this chapter is about belongs to a particular decade**, and it faded as the cars stopped being strange.

And then, nearly every time, the same second question.

*Is it safe?*

It's worth noticing where that question comes from. **It isn't hostility.** Nobody opens with the size as an accusation. They open by saying they like it — and then, having said so, they worry about it. The car is small, everything else on an American interstate isn't, and the arithmetic seems obvious. **The concern is affectionate, which is exactly why it deserves a real answer rather than a defence.**

## The answer I give

I've a short version and I've given it many times, standing next to the car.

Mercedes designed this to be safe. Just like a race car. **See the silver part? That's the safety cell.** When a race car crashes, the cell protects the driver — they pop out afterwards and hold their hands up.

I demonstrate that part. Hands up, unhurt, walking away from the wreckage.

Same thing here. A solid structure built for protection. The silver you can see running around the car in @fig-day-one isn't trim; it's the structure, and the body panels hung on it aren't.

Do they believe it? Maybe. Maybe not. **A specification does not defeat an impression**, and the impression arrived first — from twenty feet away, before anyone heard a word about safety cells. The pointing helps more than the explaining does, which tells you something about what kind of question it really is.

So I stopped relying on the engineering answer alone. What I have instead is sixteen years of driving.

## What sixteen years shows

```{r}
#| label: exposure
#| echo: false

## Boundaries come from the TRIP logs, not the fuel logs. A fill is a transaction,
## not the end of a life: TwoRed's last fill was 102 miles short of the Matson
## terminal, and Creamsicle's was 84 miles short of the handover. Between them the
## fuel record misses 186 miles -- and both cars' final journeys are exactly the
## ones it cannot see.
tw <- max(twored_legs$end_odo, na.rm = TRUE) - min(twored_fuel$Odometer)   ## 4 -> 71,283
cs <- 58987 - 30290   ## Start/Final Mileage stamps, Creamsicle_trip_clean.csv
short <- 100000 - (tw + cs)
## The prose spells these out, so guard them: a data change must break the build,
## not silently falsify a sentence.
stopifnot(nrow(twored_fuel) + nrow(cream_fuel) == 467, tw + cs == 99976, short == 24)

## TwoFer is not here. It was leased, never logged for travel, and its 1,209 Honolulu
## miles are errands, not exposure of the kind this chapter is counting.
exposure <- data.frame(
  Car   = c("TwoRed", "Creamsicle"),
  Years = c("2010-2017", "2021-2024"),
  Miles = c(tw, cs)
)
knitr::kable(
  rbind(exposure, data.frame(Car = "Total", Years = "", Miles = sum(exposure$Miles))),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = paste("Documented miles, odometer to odometer. The trip logs supply the",
                  "boundaries; the fuel logs cannot see either car's last journey.")
)
```

Add the two odometers together and they stop `r short` miles short of a hundred thousand. **That is not a rounded figure, and it is not the fuel log's figure either** — a fill is a transaction, not the end of a life, and the last drive each car ever made is one neither fuel log can see. Four hundred and sixty-seven fill-ups. Two hundred and twenty-five logged driving days. **Forty-nine mainland states, ten Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory** — the log itself only witnesses forty-five of the states, for reasons chapter 13 gets into, but the car went to all of them. Gravel on the Dalton Highway north of the Arctic Circle. Frost heaves across the Canadian plains. The Tail of the Dragon. The Oregon coast highway. Two winters and a good many summers.

No crash.

That's worth stating plainly and then immediately qualifying, because a number like that can be made to say more than it should. I'm one driver, and a prudent one. The miles are mostly interstate, mostly in daylight, and almost none of them are urban commuting. **The hundred thousand miles do not show that the car kept me safe. They show that the car did not prevent sixteen years of safe driving** — which is a smaller claim, and the honest one.

The larger claim comes from two days when the driving stopped being ordinary.

## Two close calls

### The hole in the Yukon

Before heading to Alaska, where the car would meet the challenges of the Dalton Highway, the cute wheels came off.

Smart Madness put steel rims on the car, and I bought a spare wheel to carry. It barely fitted in the rear luggage compartment. **They were quite sure I would hit something bad** — although I imagine they were thinking about something sharp rather than something deep.

Nobody told me about the flags.

Along the highway through Canada's Yukon Territory, small flags are set at the roadside to mark a pothole. I didn't know that when I started, so I learned it the way you learn most things up there, which is by hitting a few. Fortunately the lessons came from small ones. **After a while the rule is automatic: a flag on the highway's side warns to slow down and swerve.**

The car-eater had no flag.

It was big enough to swallow a car — not a wheel, a car — and it arrived with no warning at all. I saw it late and went around it.

Two things about that. The first is the one this chapter is built on: **the hole was big enough to eat a big car too.** The hazard didn't care what I was driving. **The escape did.** Something wider and heavier has a wider, heavier problem getting out of the way at speed, on a road that narrow, with a shoulder that isn't really a shoulder.

The second is about how it happened at all. **You learn the pattern. Flag equals slow and swerve. You begin to trust your experience — and the trust is earned, because the pattern is real and it holds hundreds of times.** Then once it doesn't.

**Accidents happen when the pattern doesn't hold.**

### The on-ramp near Fort Worth

I was heading east on the interstate. I left it to drive through a small town — no reason, just curious, nothing to stop for. Getting back on meant crossing over the freeway on an overpass and then taking a long sweeping left turn down onto the on-ramp.

I was most of the way around that curve when a police car came up the ramp. Full speed. No lights, no siren.

I pulled the steering wheel hard right and hit the brakes hard. TwoRed slid to a stop on the shoulder, inches from the metal guard rail.

I sat there. I was stunned, and my first thought was that I'd done something wrong — that I was the one going the wrong way. So I waited. And while I waited I watched several cars come down the on-ramp exactly as I had been doing.

It was the police car that was going the wrong direction.

Did the police stop? Of course not. This was Texas.

I missed being hit head-on by three things: quick action, some luck, and a small car. **There was not room on that shoulder for a big one to have stopped without hitting the guard rail.**

Note what was and was not available to me. Nothing about prudence prevents a vehicle coming the wrong way up a ramp with no warning; the hazard was outside my control entirely. What I had was a steering input and a braking distance, and both had to work in a very short space.

**And note that it is the same failure as the pothole.** On-ramps run one way. That is a pattern, it is real, and it holds every single time for years — which is precisely why I was around that curve at speed and not creeping. **I trusted a pattern, and the pattern didn't hold.** The sat-there-stunned part, the wondering whether I was the one going the wrong way, is what it feels like when a rule that has never failed suddenly does.

## The pattern, and what happens when it breaks

Put the two together, because they are not two stories.

Both times, the danger was not that I did something careless. **It was that the world briefly stopped behaving the way a lifetime of driving had taught me it behaves.** A hazard on that road is flagged. Traffic on an on-ramp goes one way. Both rules are sound, both are earned by long experience, and both are what let you drive at a reasonable speed instead of crawling everywhere in a state of suspicion.

You can't drive without trusting patterns. **And you can't make patterns hold.** So the only thing left to ask of a car is what it can do in the second after one breaks.



## Small and nimble are components of safety

That is the argument, and I know it runs against the intuition.

The preconception treats size as a liability to be excused — *yes, it is small, but it is well built.* I don't think that's the right shape for the answer. **In both of the moments where this car came closest to being destroyed, it was the smallness that got me out.** Less mass to move, less distance to move it through, and a chassis that answers immediately because there is not much of it.

A safety cell is for the crash you are having. **Handling is for the crash you aren't going to have** — and that second kind gets used far more often. Nobody counts those. There's no column for them, in this record or any other, which is why the two I remember are worth more here than the hundred thousand miles they sit inside.

The wide tires belong to the same argument, which is why they come next.

## The people who knew the car

Something about that period is easy to miss now. **In 2010, and for a few years after, the Smart was the hot-rodder's small car.** People tricked them out -- unusual paint, custom accessories, engine work. There was a whole scene. We did some of that ourselves, and the tires were only part of it.

The modifications are not the point. **The scene came with mechanics who actually knew the car**, and that is what we got out of it. The alternative was the Mercedes dealer, and you can guess what a dealer charges for simple maintenance.

So when the crosswind became a problem, I wasn't working it out alone. I described it to people who had heard it described before.

Every service TwoRed and Creamsicle ever had was done at that shop, in Signal Hill, California, over fourteen years and two cars -- with one exception, when something went wrong in Wisconsin and we were a long way from anybody who knew a Smart.

**And there is evidence for all of this that I did not put in the record on purpose.** Signal Hill turns up seven times in TwoRed's fuel log. Every one of them is a service visit. There is a filling station two blocks up the street, and after a service there was usually a hundred-mile drive back to Lake San Marcos, so it made sense to leave with a full tank.

**A fuel log turns out to be a record of who looked after the car, and not only of where it went.**

## The one modification, and what it cost

The first crossing was made on the stock narrow tires — the ones a car like this leaves the factory with, sized for a city.

Crossing the deserts, a strong wind would come from the side. It pushed the car enough that staying in the lane could be a challenge. **And the difficulty was not the strength of it. It was that the push was not constant.** It varied, so I had to keep correcting — a small input, then another, then another, for as long as the wind lasted.

It was possible to control. But it was tiring.

**That distinction is the whole of it, and it is worth holding on to, because this book comes back to it.** A steady force you lean against and forget. A varying one you have to answer, continuously, and the cost is not in any single correction but in the fact that they never stop. **The wind wasn't dangerous. Being tired at 70 miles an hour is.**

It happened enough that I raised it with them. They understood right away, and they had the solution: wider tires.

The fancy rims came along with them, because this is a car that is fun to drive and fun to be seen in. It worked. The handling became very good.

![The same car after Smart Madness had finished with it. Set this against @fig-day-one: the tires are visibly wider, and the fancy rims came along with them.](images/TwoRed/twored_wide_wheels.jpg){#fig-wide-wheels}

Now, when I pull up behind a high-priced sports car, I note the width of their tires. Mine aren't as wide. **But they are wide enough to take care of the problem.**

**The wheels were never about fuel.** They were bought for control in a crosswind, which is to say they were bought for safety. But wider tires have a theoretical cost — more rolling resistance, more frontal area. The effect ought to be small, and it ought to be there.

So the fuel log gets asked a question it was never keeping score on. `r n_nar` fill-ups on the narrow tires, `r n_wid` on the wide ones, with the winter-tire interval cut out entirely because three things changed on it at once.

Here is what four reasonable ways of asking produce.

```{r}
#| label: wheels
#| echo: false
tr <- twored_fuel
tr$wheels <- ifelse(tr$Odometer < 13510, "narrow",
              ifelse(tr$Odometer >= 34190 & tr$Odometer <= 39739, "xice", "wide"))
## The winter-tire interval is documented at both ends (Madness Autoworks receipt #5951)
## and dropped outright: tire size, tire compound and tire pressure all changed on it,
## inside a single trip. See data/TwoRed/wheel_states.csv.
d <- tr[tr$wheels != "xice" & is.finite(tr$mpg) & is.finite(tr$leg_miles) &
          !isTRUE(tr$partial_fill), ]
d$wide <- as.integer(d$wheels == "wide")
n_nar <- sum(d$wide == 0); n_wid <- sum(d$wide == 1)

pct <- function(fit, dat) {
  b <- coef(fit)[["wide"]]; ci <- confint(fit)["wide", ]
  mu <- mean(dat$mpg[dat$wide == 0])
  sprintf("%+.1f%% [%+.1f, %+.1f]", 100*b/mu, 100*ci[1]/mu, 100*ci[2]/mu)
}
dw <- d[abs(d$Odometer - 13510) <= 12000, ]   ## a local window around the change

wheel_tab <- data.frame(
  `How the question is asked` = c("raw difference", "controlling for leg length",
      "leg length and odometer trend", "local window, +/-12,000 miles"),
  `Effect on economy` = c(
      pct(lm(mpg ~ wide, data = d), d),
      pct(lm(mpg ~ wide + leg_miles, data = d), d),
      pct(lm(mpg ~ wide + leg_miles + Odometer, data = d), d),
      pct(lm(mpg ~ wide + leg_miles, data = dw), dw)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(wheel_tab, caption = paste(
  "Four defensible ways of asking the same question of the same", nrow(d),
  "fill-ups. 95% intervals."))
```

**Look at the signs.** Positive, more positive, negative, negative — and every interval contains zero. Not one of those rows is wrong. They are four defensible ways of handling the same fill-ups, and they do not agree on whether the wide tires helped or hurt.

**That is not a cautious result. A cautious result is a small number with a tight interval.** This is an unstable one, and the instability has a cause. `r n_nar` rows against `r n_wid`, and the `r n_nar` are not a sample of ordinary driving. They are the car's first ten months: one crossing, one season, one part of the country. Every difference between that year and the fifteen that followed is riding along with the wheel change, and no amount of controlling pulls them apart.

**I could have picked one.** Any single row of that table, printed on its own, would have looked like an answer. That is exactly why the table is here instead.


The one thing the table does rule out is a large effect. Nothing in it is consistent with the wheels costing ten per cent. Beyond that it declines to say, and I am not going to make it.

**The one change ever made to this car was made for safety.** What it cost at the pump is a question this record cannot settle — and knowing that is worth more than a number I would have had to choose.

## Attention is a component of safety too

Everything above is about the car. But the most important safety variable on a long day isn't the car at all. It's whether I'm still paying attention at hour eight.

When Nancy's along we talk, mostly. That works, and it works well.

Alone is the harder problem, and my answer was audio books. Captivating ones -- the kind that keep you on the edge of the seat. You can listen and drive; the two go together rather than compete for the same attention. I mixed them with Radio Lab episodes, preloaded on the phone and played through the car speakers.

There were days I arrived at my destination and didn't want to stop. I had to hear more of the book. It got to the point where I wanted to drive, so that I could listen to something interesting.

Now the part that actually matters, because it's the part that generalises. **I wasn't being interrupted.** No calls, no messages, nobody at the door, nothing waiting for an answer. Hours of it. That's what let me follow a story properly, and following a story properly is what kept me alert.

Which turns the usual worry inside out. The hazard on a long drive isn't stimulation. It's monotony -- the tree tunnels of the road chapter, the fast unremarkable miles that turn out later to have been the worst ones. **A good story is the countermeasure, and a car is one of the last places left where you can give one your whole attention without something interrupting.**

It's audio, and that isn't a caveat I'm adding afterwards. Eyes on the road and hands on the wheel is the condition that makes the whole thing work.

## What this chapter cannot tell you

Granted: no crash testing.

Nothing here is a substitute for a barrier test, and nothing here can answer the question people are really asking, which is what happens in the collision. I haven't had one. That's the whole of my evidence and it's also the limit of it. **A record of things that didn't happen can't tell you what it would've been like if they had.**

What I can say is narrower and, I think, more useful. Within sight of a hundred thousand documented miles, on gravel and frost heave and interstate and coast highway, the small car was twice the reason the day ended without damage. Both times, the thing that saved it was the thing everyone worries about.
